slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open by explaining the second pillar: coordinates turn geometry into algebra. Instead of ruler-and-compass, we now locate points by numbers and describe figures by equations. This makes distance, intersection, and angle computable. Orient students to printed pages 46 through 64.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the four themes. Students should leave able to write equations for lines in slope-intercept and general form, compute distances and midpoints with formulas, find circle-line and line-line intersections algebraically, and classify isometries as translations, rotations, reflections, or glide reflections.

slides.label: Cartesian Plane
slides.narration: Introduce the Cartesian coordinate system: a number line for each axis, an ordered pair for each point. Emphasize that this single idea turns every geometric question into an algebraic question and every algebraic identity into a geometric theorem.

slides.label: Line Equations
slides.narration: Present line equations in slope-intercept and general form. Slope measures rise over run and encodes the angle a line makes with the horizontal. Lines are parallel when slopes are equal, perpendicular when slopes are negative reciprocals.

slides.label: Distance Formula
slides.narration: Derive the distance formula from the Pythagorean theorem applied to a right triangle with legs parallel to the axes. Then show that the midpoint is the average of coordinates.

slides.label: Circle-Line Intersection
slides.narration: Show how to find where a line meets a circle by substituting the line equation into the circle equation and solving the resulting quadratic. The discriminant tells the count: two intersections, one tangency, or no meeting.

slides.label: Isometry Classification
slides.narration: Introduce the isometry classification theorem: every distance-preserving map of the plane is a translation, rotation, reflection, or glide reflection. Coordinates make this classification possible because each isometry has a specific matrix-plus-translation form.

slides.label: Three Reflections
slides.narration: Present the three-reflections theorem: every isometry can be written as a composition of at most three reflections. Translations and rotations use two reflections; glide reflections use three. This factorization shows that reflections are the atoms of Euclidean symmetry.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter by connecting coordinates, distance, intersection, and isometry classification into a single algebraic framework. The coordinate method does not replace Euclid; it translates Euclid into a language where computation can assist and verify every proof.
